items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: A hotel with infinite rooms, all full, can always take more guests
items.claim: Hilbert's Hotel has rooms numbered 1, 2, 3, ... Every room is occupied. A new guest arrives and you can give them a room. An infinite bus arrives and you can house them all. Infinitely many infinite buses arrive and you can still house all of them.
items.prompt: How do you fit one more guest into a full infinite hotel?

options.text: Move every guest from room n to room n+1; this frees up room 1 for the new guest; the original guests still all have rooms
You need a special infinite room

items.reveal:
David Hilbert constructed the hotel to illustrate counter-intuitive properties of countable infinity. For a finite hotel, full means full. For a countably infinite hotel, 'full' is not the same as 'no spare capacity'.

One new guest: shift every guest from n to n+1. Room 1 frees up.
Infinite new guests (one bus): shift every existing guest from n to 2n. All odd rooms (1, 3, 5, ...) free up — infinitely many.
Countably many buses, each with countably many guests: use prime powers. Existing guest goes to 2 to the n. Guest k from bus m goes to (the m+2-th prime) to the k. All housed.

This tells you about cardinality of countable sets: adding any countable collection to a countable set produces a countable set, of the same cardinality.

What the hotel CAN'T do: house the uncountable infinity of reals. Cantor's diagonal argument shows you'd run out of rooms.
items.why: Infinity is treated as a single concept. Hilbert's hotel reveals that countable infinity has very different properties from finite quantity — and from uncountable infinity.

items.title: The set of all sets that don't contain themselves
items.claim: Define R as the set of all sets that don't contain themselves. Does R contain itself? If yes — then by definition it doesn't. If no — then by definition it does. Russell discovered this in 1901 and broke set theory.
items.prompt: How did mathematicians fix the problem?

options.text: By restricting what can be a 'set' — modern Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms (ZFC) only allow forming sets in specific controlled ways (separation, replacement, union, power set), and you can't form 'the set of all sets'
By ignoring sets that contain themselves

items.reveal:
Gottlob Frege spent decades building arithmetic from formal logic. His Grundgesetze (Vol II, 1903) was at the printer when Bertrand Russell wrote to him pointing out the paradox. Frege added a despairing postscript: 'A scientist can hardly meet with anything more undesirable than to have the foundation give way just as the work is finished.'

The paradox: define R = {x : x is not an element of x}. Is R in R?
- If R is in R, then by R's definition R is not in R. Contradiction.
- If R is not in R, then R satisfies the criterion to be in R. Contradiction.

Resolution: in ZFC, the axiom schema of separation only allows forming {x in A : phi(x)} from an EXISTING set A. You can't form 'all sets such that phi'. There is no universal set.

The Barber's paradox (the barber shaves all who don't shave themselves; does he shave himself?) is a pop-culture version.
items.why: Naive set theory looks intuitive — define a set by any property. Russell showed this leads directly to contradiction, and modern set theory had to carefully restrict what counts as a set.
